title: Blessing others
hook: the Guru asks for the dust of the feet of the Sikh who remembers and helps others remember (Gauri Var M4, ang 306)

segments.voice: Yesterday, after the morning: sitting and standing, with breath and mouthful, the Name comes along to work. Your line was work, remembering. Did your cue come around, and did a breath remember? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-four.

Shoes come off at the door of a gurdwara. In some gurdwaras, volunteers take them, line them up, even wipe the dust off, and the person doing it might be a shopkeeper, a student, or someone with a great deal of money. Dust from other people's feet, handled as an honor. Hold that picture, because Guru Ram Das ends his salok about the Gursikh's day with dust. And the surprise is who's asking for it. Today: the last lines, and a blessing that runs the wrong way.
screen: `SHOES OFF AT THE DOOR.` → `DUST, HANDLED AS AN HONOR.` → `WHO'S ASKING FOR IT?`

segments.voice: Here are the salok's closing lines, paraphrased. The one on whom my Lord is kind, to that Gursikh the Guru gives the teaching. Servant Nanak asks for the dust of the feet of that Gursikh who repeats the Name himself, and leads others to repeat it. Read it slowly, because it turns things upside down. The voice here is the Guru's, signing with the name Nanak, as the Gurus do in the Granth, and calling himself servant. And the Guru is the one asking. He asks for the dust of a disciple's feet. Touching someone's feet is a gesture of deep respect in Punjab. Asking for the dust from them goes lower still. Next, notice which Sikh he honors this way. The earlier lines already called the Sikh who rises early and remembers through the working day pleasing to the Guru's mind. But the one whose dust the Guru asks for is the one who remembers and then helps someone else remember. The salok has been walking outward all along: from one person waking, to a day of work, to other people. And notice the first line here: the teaching comes as kindness. The Gursikh doesn't earn it like a wage. The Lord is kind, and the Guru shares the teaching. So helping someone else remember isn't a lecture or a recruiting drive. It's passing on a kindness you were given. A reminder on a hard day. A line of a hymn sent to a friend. An invitation to sit together. That's the kind of Sikh, in this salok, whose dust the Guru wants.
screen: `SERVANT NANAK ASKS FOR THE DUST.` · `THE GURU BOWS TO THE DISCIPLE.` · `REMEMBER, THEN HELP OTHERS REMEMBER.` · `PASSING ON A KINDNESS.` · then, large: `BLESSING OTHERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help one person remember. In the sit, let the breath slow, and let one person come to mind who could use a reminder today: of something good, of someone who loves them, of a line that once steadied you. Don't plan a speech. Choose one small, kind way to pass it on: a message, a call, a line of Gurbani if they'd welcome it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out, and hold that person in it. The bell holds the time.
Blessing others. The salok's last line: servant Nanak asks for the dust of the feet of the Sikh who remembers the Name and helps others remember it. Today's word.
Your line: help others remember. Send the one message you chose in the sit, before the day gets away from you. Keep it short. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs meet this salok when Gauri ki Var is sung or read, and it is quoted when Sikhs speak of the Gursikh's day; looking after shoes at the gurdwara door is one of the forms of seva Sikhs volunteer for.

fork.setup: a Sikh rises early, remembers through the workday, and then helps a friend remember too. what does the salok's last line do?
options: tells the Sikh to bow lower.
has the Guru ask for that Sikh's dust.
fork.reveal: servant Nanak asks for the dust of the feet of that Gursikh: the blessing runs from the Guru to the disciple.

original.note: dust: in the salok, the dust of a Gursikh's feet, asked for by the Guru.

trapdoor: what you thought: a blessing flows down, from teacher to student.
what it means: here the Guru asks a blessing of the student who helps others remember.

notes: Closing lines of the salok 'gur satgur ka jo sikh akhaae' (Gauri ki Var M4, Ang 305–306), paraphrased from memory; please confirm wording and Ang 306.
The hook says that in some gurdwaras volunteers look after and wipe shoes (joda ghar seva); please confirm the description.
'Touching someone's feet is a gesture of deep respect in Punjab' is a cultural statement, not from the cited text; please confirm or cut.
'Signing with the name Nanak, as the Gurus do in the Granth' refers to the Gurus whose hymns are in the Granth; please confirm the wording is acceptable.
Editor: the teach no longer implies the earlier lines withhold the Guru's favor; the salok already calls that Sikh pleasing to the Guru's mind.
